summary: SIP sets up sessions between pairs of user agents, so two-party calls are straightforward, but conferences with many participants need more. This document is a framework for how SIP can support conferencing. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Phone calls usually have two people. This sketches how an internet phone system can host a group call where many people join one meeting.

questions: how does sip handle conference calls
what is a sip conference focus
what is a loosely coupled conference
subtitle: How SIP can run a multi-party conference: one focus in the middle, mixers for the media, and a policy that decides who joins.

tldr.problem: SIP dialogs connect pairs of user agents, so a call between two people is obvious, but a conversation among many participants is not.
tldr.mechanism: A central user agent called the focus keeps a SIP dialog with every participant, enforces a conference policy and uses mixers to combine the media, forming a star topology around a conference URI.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a framework of architecture, terminology and components. It points to other specifications for the detailed mechanisms.

facts.label: Conference URI
facts.value: Always a SIP or SIPS URI

today: RFC 4353 is an Informational framework from February 2006. According to the metadata it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Kinds of Multi-Party Conferences
sections.content:
SIP can support several models of multi-party communication. In a loosely coupled conference, participants use a multicast media group, there is no signaling relationship among them and no central point of control. In a fully distributed conference, every participant has SIP signaling with every other. That model is outside this document.

This RFC covers the tightly coupled conference, where each participant connects to one central point of control that provides conference functions and may also mix media. RFC 3261 does not directly address these conferences, although basic participation works without extra protocol support. The framework aims to meet the requirements in RFC 4245.
sections.eli5: People can talk as a crowd in a big hall where nobody is in charge, or each can call every other person, or everyone can call one host. This memo is about the third way.

sections.title: The Focus and the Conference URI
sections.content:
The focus is a SIP user agent that sits in the middle and keeps a SIP dialog with each participant, which produces a star topology. It makes sure the media streams of the conference reach everyone, using one or more mixers, and it enforces the conference policy, which can be thought of as a database of rules for how the conference operates.

A conference is identified by a conference URI, which identifies its focus. Every conference has a unique focus and a unique URI, and requests to that URI are routed to the focus and only the focus. The URI is always a SIP or SIPS URI, and it is opaque: you cannot tell from its shape that it names a focus. The isfocus feature tag from callee capabilities can reveal that a user agent is acting as a focus. Ideally users learn the URI from an email, instant message or web page instead of guessing it.

Participants may be conference-unaware, meaning the focus looks like any other user agent to them. They can still join and leave using SIP. A conference-aware participant can also subscribe to the conference notification service and use non-SIP mechanisms to reach the policy.
sections.eli5: Everyone dials the same phone number, and the host on the other end holds all the calls together. Some guests do not even know it is a group call, and that is fine.

sections.title: The Elements and What They Do
sections.content:
The focus checks policy when it receives an INVITE. It can reject the caller, or hold the INVITE while a moderator is notified and approves. It removes a participant by sending a BYE (ejection), adds one by sending an INVITE, and changes media by sending a re-INVITE or UPDATE with a new offer. How it interprets policy is local and not standardized.

A mixer combines media streams into one or more output streams. It is not aware of a conference as such, and is always under a focus's control, directly or through delegation to participants. The conference policy server is a logical interface between clients and the policy, reached by a non-SIP mechanism. The conference notification service is the focus acting as a notifier: it accepts subscriptions to the conference URI and reports changes in participants and their dialogs. Anonymous participants can have their identity withheld or be omitted from the notifications.

Any SIP user agent with a dialog to the focus is a participant, including a PC application, a hardphone, a PSTN gateway or another focus. A conference whose participant is the focus of another conference is a simplex cascaded conference.
sections.eli5: The host keeps the guest list, the sound mixer blends voices, and a notice board tells people who has come and gone. The rule book can be as simple as a list of allowed names or as complicated as time-of-day rules.

sections.title: Common Operations
sections.content:
Creating a conference builds a focus, a conference policy and a unique conference URI together. Uniqueness can be guaranteed by keeping records, generating URIs algorithmically or choosing random URIs with a low chance of collision. New policies start with implementation-dependent defaults, and changing them uses a non-SIP mechanism. In an ad-hoc conference, one endpoint decides to become the focus and moves existing dialogs over with a re-INVITE or UPDATE that carries the new conference URI. The Join header can also ask a user agent to create one.

To join, a participant sends an INVITE to the conference URI, or uses the Join header against a dialog it learned about. Third parties can add someone with REFER, sent either to the participant or to the focus. Leaving is a BYE, and the focus then makes sure the departed participant stops receiving media. SIP has no explicit way to destroy a conference. It happens as a by-product, for example when the policy says the conference ends when the last or a specific user leaves.

Membership can be learned by subscribing to the notification service. Adding or removing media takes a re-INVITE using offer/answer, and the focus issues its own re-INVITEs to the others. Announcements and recordings are modeled as an application that joins as a participant and sends media to the mixer like anyone else.
sections.eli5: A person joins by calling the host and leaves by hanging up. Someone can also ask the host to ring a friend. A recorded voice that says who joined is just another guest who happens to be a machine.

sections.title: Ways to Build a Conference System
sections.content:
The RFC describes five physical realizations of the logical pieces.

  • Centralized server: one box holds the focus, policy server and mixers.
  • Endpoint server: user A, already in a call with B, becomes a focus, changes its URI by re-INVITE, and invites C. The external interfaces are the same as for a central server.
  • Media server component: an application server owns the policies and acts as the top-level focus, while a separate mixing server only mixes media on its instructions.
  • Distributed mixing: a central focus, but each endpoint has its own mixer. Media can go multi-unicast (N-1 streams), via a shared multicast group, or via a central point that redistributes by multicast.
  • Cascaded mixers: for very large conferences, many mixers are spread through the network. Each participant connects to exactly one, and the focus links the mixers with a control protocol.
sections.eli5: You can put everything in one big room, let one guest act as host, split the jobs between two rooms, let each guest do their own blending, or chain many small rooms together for a huge crowd.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Conferences need authorization, such as limits on who may join or create new policies, and authorization needs authentication. The RFC says normal SIP authentication mechanisms should suffice. Privacy matters too: some users want to listen in silently, and others only want to hide their identity while others know they are present. The conferencing system needs to provide these functions.
sections.eli5: The host must be sure who is allowed in, and some guests may want to listen quietly or keep their name private.
